utterances.text: No. They never stopped any vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about pedestrians? Did they ever stop pedestrians?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, no pedestrian was ever stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they ever set up roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did they ever set up any roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they never set up any roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they ever stop persons in any manner to check for identification?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No. Our patrols did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had you ever received or had the police ever received any complaints about those vehicles that were -- the people in the vehicles that were watching, observing what was happening in the town?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not receive any complaints. Quite the contrary. The citizens themselves commended us in a way. They said that they felt much more secure knowing that there were such patrols around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had they ever made any citizen arrests of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they never arrested anyone, because it was not their task to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about disarming anyone? Did they ever disarm or remove a weapon from anyone?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: They never disarmed anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So they were just your eyes and ears on the roadway, if you want to call it that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that was their only task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these vehicular patrols, did you have any other, let's say, foot patrols or patrols outside of these roadways during the evenings?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were night-time patrols in the town that had the same task as the daytime patrols, that is, to walk around the town. They were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, is it time now for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I keep looking at the clock on the screen. Anyway, we can have our break and resume at 1805.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Now, when we left off before the break, we were talking about walking patrols, or foot patrols, and these were in the night-time and they were similar to the same type of patrols you had during the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And one of these patrols, or a foot patrol would consist of how many people during the night-time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how many evening foot patrols were there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: There were two patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these foot patrols, during the evening, were they wearing any type of uniform or any type of special clothing to differentiate themselves from the public?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the two vehicular patrols that were watching people entering and leaving Bosanski Samac? And you indicated that each of those vehicle patrols had three people in the car. Were any of those six people between the two cars armed? I'm sorry. Were any of those six people between the two cars wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No. They also did not wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these foot patrols, as best you know, was the public aware of these foot patrols during the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they stop people on the street as part of these patrols?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not stop people on the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about stopping vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not stop vehicles either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they ever approach citizens for an identification check?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not approach citizens for an identification check.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What would these people be doing?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: They would monitor the town, what was happening in the town, what others were doing in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if anything significant happened, who would they contact?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: They would contact me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, between the two checkpoints, or these foot patrols, was there any liaison that would go between them during the evening, liaison or a middle person, if you want to call them, that would go between the two checkpoints or between the foot patrols, to make sure that everything was all right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a special personal vehicle that travelled from one patrol to the other, from the one that was at the hospital to the other patrol that was by the two cemeteries. This was a personal vehicle which had a connection to both patrols, and also with the patrol that was in the town, and this person would ask if there was any news, any observations, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the vehicles that were used at the two evening patrols, were these private vehicles or were they military vehicles of some sort? What type of vehicles were they?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: This was a private passenger car. The private cars belonging to the people were used, the people that were in the patrol that night. We didn't have any military cars or other state vehicles. These were privately owned vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there ever any sort of insignia on the vehicle to indicate that it was part of this independent military unit?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, there was no insignia on any of the cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did these patrols last? They started, according to your testimony, in the fall or the late fall -- mid- to late fall of 1991. How long did they last?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: These patrols lasted until the aggression, that is to say, the occupation of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So until April 17th of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, at the same time that you have these patrols, were there any Serb patrols or checkpoints in Bosanski Samac and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were Serb checkpoints in Bosanski Samac and in the surrounding towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were the checkpoints? Please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: One checkpoint was at the main road between Sarajevo and Samac, close to the silo; the other checkpoint was in the local commune of Crkvina, which is also on this main road Samac-Sarajevo; then there was a control point on the regional road Samac-Orasje, in the local commune of Srpska Tisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who manned these patrols, these Serbian patrols or checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: These checkpoints that I mentioned, and I said they were on the main road, were manned by the JNA members and also the military police of the former JNA, and the checkpoint on the regional road Samac-Orasje, in the local commune of Srpska Tisina, was mostly manned by the villagers, Serbs, and of course they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was the 4th Detachment involved in any of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was not involved with the checkpoints on the main road Samac-Sarajevo, nor was it involved with the checkpoint on the regional road. Members of some other detachment were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were these checkpoints similar to your patrols, where they just would sit there and observe what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not similar at all to our checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell us: How were they different from your checkpoints? What were they doing at these three Serb checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Contrary to our points, which were just observing and monitoring what was happening and who was passing by, these checkpoints that I said were on the main road of Samac to Sarajevo, and the regional road, Samac-Orasje, people on these checkpoints would stop personal vehicles - cars, trucks - they would ask people for their ID cards, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would they stop buses?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would also stop buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would they enter the buses and ask for identification cards?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would enter buses and ask for ID cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How were Muslims and Croats treated at these identification points - I'm sorry - at these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: After they determined that they were dealing with a Croat or a Muslim who was passing these roads, the vehicles belonging to these people would be searched. They would have to open up the trunk. They would take a look at what was being carried and transferred, and so on. They would take a look at what kind of material was being transferred. The trunk of the car would have to be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were these people treated properly and respectfully during these searches?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: I have information that they did not treat them properly and respectfully, that they treated them with disrespect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If a person was stopped and they were of Serb ethnicity, how would they be treated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Those that they knew personally, they would just let them go, and others, if they determined that the people were Serbs, would also be let go. They would not search their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were tolls ever requested, tolls or bribes, in order to pass through this checkpoint or these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a toll had to be paid on the main road Samac-Sarajevo. On this other local checkpoint in Srpska Tisina sometimes certain things would be taken away, things that were valuable, but the tolls were not collected, not on the regional road, but it was collected on the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to this toll money that was collected, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: This toll money that was collected would go to the Serbian Democratic Party, which financed its military from this money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I presume we are going to find out what is the basis of the information that Mr. Fitozovic has concerning all of these points that have just been made?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to -- let's start off with the tolls being collected. How were you made aware that tolls were being collected, or whatever you want to call them, charges, tolls, bribes, were being collected by people at one of these checkpoints? Let's start off with that.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: I found out about them from people that paid the tolls. And the price wasn't set. It wasn't a fixed price. People had to pay whatever they were asked to pay, whether it was a bus or a personal car or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the next question is: How did you know -- or how did you learn that the money that was being collected, these charges or tolls, went to the Serbian political party?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: I found out about this from the members of the 4th Detachment. Some of them informed me regularly on what was happening there. The 4th Detachment also paid its members from this money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me -- I was going to discuss this a little bit later, but let's take this issue up now. At some point after the 4th Detachment was established, did you have one or more informers, if you want to call them, within the 4th Detachment that was providing you with information as to what was happening in that unit?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning I had two men who were in the 4th Detachment who regularly informed me on things. Later, as time went by, as the end of the year was nearing and also as the aggression was coming closer, so the number of the people was increasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, a few last questions concerning these patrols or checkpoints, Serbian checkpoints. How were these people dressed at these checkpoints, the people who were manning them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: The people on the main road were dressed in typical, if I may say so, uniforms of the JNA. Those on the checkpoint that was in Srpska Tisina were sometimes dressed in camouflage uniforms and sometimes they wore civilian clothes, but they always had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were the weapons visible?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the weapons were visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue on to December of 1991. Did something happen to your job in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of 1991, on the 24th of December, to be exact, I stopped working at my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you voluntarily stop working or were you laid off?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't stop working voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did someone tell you why you were being laid off or let go?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was told first that I was not fulfilling the conditions for that job because you needed the seventh level for that kind of work, so I wasn't fulfilling the conditions and I was laid off, although I did all the work and I worked there for eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say you needed this seventh level, do you mean you needed a full engineering degree to handle that position as a chief?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had to have an engineering degree, which I didn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you had worked in that position for, you indicated, for eight years. And how long had you worked at that company? I know some of it was off and on. How long had you worked at the power distribution plant?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: All together, I worked there for 12 years. Of that, I was a manager for 11 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the person who replaced you, he was of what ethnic group? He belonged to what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he belong to any political parties?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What political party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: He belonged to the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was the national leader of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Vojislav Seselj, the Duke, was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "Duke," did he give himself the title of being a Chetnik duke?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he gave the title to himself or perhaps somebody from abroad had promoted him to that title.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, this individual who replaced you, did he have an engineering degree or was he at that seventh level of education, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not meet the requirements for the post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us continue in December of 1991. Do you recall being called to a reserve officers' meeting, being called to attend a reserve officers' meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In December I was called to the memorial home. Mitar Mihajlovic [As interpreted], Uco, to attend a meeting of the reserve officers of the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone there representing the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Representing the JNA there was Colonel Nikolic, then there was also Captain Petrovic. I'm not quite sure about his name. There was also Milos Bogdanovic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, where was Simo Zaric in relation to Colonel Nikolic? No, no. Where was he sitting in relation to Colonel Nikolic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: He sat right next to him. But I didn't quite understand why Simo Zaric was there at all, because he did not belong to the group of the reserve officers. As far as I know, he was not a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about this meeting. Just first list the names. Who were the speakers at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the first person to speak was Milos Bogdanovic, then Colonel Nikolic spoke. The captain that I mentioned also spoke, and so did Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what Colonel Nikolic said when he spoke?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: He said more or less the following: That there are enough weapons, that there are enough men, but they felt that there weren't enough officers, and that's why they had set up the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In response to his -- or in addition to his comment of there not being enough officers, military officers, even though they have enough weapons and men, did he ask for anything?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: He asked that all the reserve officers present there to place themselves at the disposal of the 17th Tactical Group, each in the specialty that they were trained for, where they would be in command and control of certain units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, why were you there? Is it because -- or why don't you tell me. Why were you at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: I was there because I was also a reserve officer, but I belonged to the so-called JNA reserve, whereas most of the others belonged to -- were the reserve officers of the former TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what the captain, Milos Bogdanovic, said at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that Milos Bogdanovic was a captain. At that time he was the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I meant what either Milos Bogdanovic or what the captain said that you thought had the name of Petrovic. Do you recall what they said to the reserve officers who were in attendance?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: They spoke about the necessity to involve the officers in the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, do you recall what the defendant Simo Zaric said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: When Simo Zaric took the floor, he said that it was a multi-ethnic unit, a unit that would defend Bosanski Samac against any attempts to occupy it, particularly by the Zengas from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he refer to any other groups?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he refer to the unit that he was talking about that was supposed to be this multi-ethnic army to protect Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time that I heard the official title "the 4th Detachment," and Zaric said that the 4th Detachment was also a multi-ethnic unit and that its goal is to protect Bosanski Samac against any kind of occupation or attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, as you've testified, the 4th Detachment was in fact established. Did the 4th Detachment ever protect the town of Bosanski Samac against outside forces?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Up until that time that we're talking about, that's December, the 4th Detachment didn't have to defend Bosanski Samac against anyone, because Bosanski Samac did not come under an attack until the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you mean --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, did the 4th Detachment protect the town of Bosanski Samac against outside forces?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No. The 4th Detachment did not defend Bosanski Samac against outside forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the 4th Detachment, in April, defend and protect all of the inhabitants of Bosanski Samac, as Simo Zaric said it would?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No. The 4th Detachment did not defend all the inhabitants of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the 4th Detachment defend Bosanski Samac against -- or the citizens of Bosanski Samac against the Serb paramilitaries, just like Simo Zaric said it would?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No. The 4th Detachment did not defend Bosanski Samac against the units that attacked Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did it defend the town of Bosanski Samac against looting of houses?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not defend the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the 4th Detachment participate with the paramilitaries and the JNA in the takeover of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did participate in the occupation of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With the paramilitaries and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the paramilitaries and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On that evening, did you enlist or re-enlist, as invited by Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I realise you were not called, but did you enlist yourself in response to that invitation, to be a full-time active officer?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: At that meeting in December, I did not want to join the units that were subordinate to the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was clear. The army was Serbian. They were armed. The officers were all Serbs. There were just a few of us Muslims and Croats there at the meeting, because it wasn't possible for more of them to be present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said -- I just want to ask you one question based on your answer. You said it wasn't possible for more of them to be present there. Why was it impossible for more Muslims and Croats to be at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't possible because in fact there weren't more of them, because there weren't enough Muslims and Croats that had undergone requisite training in the reserve force. So the officers from these two ethnic groups simply did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why weren't Muslims and Croats being given the requisite training at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: The training took many years. I guess that at the time, in the Communist system, this was what was required. On the other hand, perhaps Croats and Muslims were not interested to pursue it. But the most important thing is that over a very long period of time, many years, nobody sent them to receive such training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's my question: Why weren't these people sent? Were they not sent because they were Croat and Muslim or were they not sent for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- or probably because they were Muslims and Croats. It was a policy that was not in existence for a long time, but it is impossible to become a reserve officer in a month or two, or a year. The reserve officers are created over a long period of years. For instance, from being a private to the rank of captain, it took me seven years. Perhaps in the seven years no other Muslim had served in that type of unit in the former JNA. They simply did not receive the training for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Fitozovic, I wonder whether you could tell us who was doing the sending of these people in terms of reserve training. When I say "who," I don't necessarily mean an exact person, but who was in charge? What category of person was in charge of picking out who should be sent to do the reserve training? This is all concerned with Mr. Weiner's question at page 76, line 22, concerning why these people weren't sent for training. So if we could have some clarification who was making those decisions, what category of person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In addition -- before you answer that question, in addition, if you can also cover the period concerning this aspect of your evidence. During which period are we discussing this training or lack of training for certain types of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to say how is it that one becomes a reserve officer. One becomes a reserve officer by first of all doing the regular national service over many years. In order to become a reserve officer in the course of one's regular national service, one has to attend a special school, which was called the reserve officers' school, and there were various schools for various arms: Artillery, infantry, engineer corps, and so on. So you undergo this training in the course of your regular national service. After the completion of the national service, the person that graduated from the reserve officers' school is awarded a certain rank once he leaves the military. As a rule, the rank is that of a second lieutenant. Then that person receives his or her assignment from the Secretariat for National Defence, either in the regular troops of the JNA or in the regular forces of the Territorial Defence. In a period of, let's say, two or three years, if there is any -- if that person undergoes any training, he or she receives a higher rank, which in the JNA was that of a lieutenant. After a certain period of time holding that rank, and after some additional training and, let's say, attendance at exercises, the person receives the rank of a captain. So it takes a long time for a person to become a reserve officer. It is impossible for somebody who did not attend the reserve officers' school to become a reserve officer, and there is no course -- for instance, somebody would say, "Okay. You take this course and then you will become a captain." That was not the system. As for the other question regarding the time period required for a person to become the reserve officer - I'm referring to the time period beginning with the end of the Second World War, when people started doing their national service, some people attended the reserve officers' school, and so a new contingent would attend the school every year, from entire Yugoslavia, and that process was going on until 1991. So that would be my response to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just to follow that up: Who made the decision as to whether or not a person would be sent to reserve officer school?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: This was decided in the Secretariat for National Defence, in the municipalities, regions, republics, and also at the level of the former Yugoslav state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And why at this level were Muslims and Croats not being sent by the Secretariat of National Defence? Why weren't they sending Croats to reserve officer school?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really answer your question. It may have been the policy in the League of Communists, but I really don't know. I don't know. I had the opportunity to be selected, and I did attend the reserve officers' school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's only about two minutes to go. Could we break here before we start in 1992 as we move on with his testimony? I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
